scenes.narration: A stack is like a vertical pile of plates where you can only add or remove items from the very top.
Think of a stack of plates on a table: you can only add a new plate to the top, and you must take the top plate off first.
The key rule is last in, first out. Adding an item is called push, and removing the top item is called pop.
Push 12 onto the stack. The top is now 12 and the size is 1.
We push 24 onto the stack. The top is now 24.
We push 36 onto the stack. The top is now 36.
We pop 36 off the top. 36 was the last one in, so it leaves first. The top is now 24.
Stacks are used everywhere in computers, such as the undo button in text editors and tracking function calls.
Takeaways: add items on top, take items off the top, and the newest item always leaves first.

scenes.narration: What is the time complexity of bubble sort, and why? Let's count the work it really does as the list grows.
We measure time by counting comparisons: the main work bubble sort does. Here are n = 4 values: Array is now [5, 1, 4, 2].
Pass 1: 5 and 1 swap, 5 and 4 swap, 5 and 2 swap. 3 comparisons. 5 is now in its final place. Array is now [1, 4, 2, 5].
Pass 2: 1 and 4 stay, 4 and 2 swap. 2 comparisons, 3 + 2 = 5 so far. 4 is now in its final place. Array is now [1, 2, 4, 5].
Pass 3: 1 and 2 stay. 1 comparison, 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 so far. No swaps in this pass. Array is now [1, 2, 4, 5], and the list is sorted.
Add up the passes: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 comparisons, which is n(n - 1) / 2 = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6. For any n, the passes make (n - 1) + (n - 2) + ... + 1, which adds up to n(n - 1) / 2.

Big O keeps only the fastest-growing part: n(n - 1) / 2 is about n² / 2, and we drop the 1/2, so bubble sort is O(n²), quadratic time, which means the work grows with n squared. In plain words: double the items and the work grows about 4 times.
Counted for real: n = 4 needs 6 comparisons, n = 8 needs 28, n = 16 needs 120, and n = 100 needs 4950. From n = 8 to n = 16, the work grows about 4 times.
Best case: an already sorted list, [1, 2, 4, 5]. Pass 1 makes 3 comparisons and no swaps, so bubble sort stops early: n - 1 = 3, which is O(n): the work grows with n, not with n².
Worst case: a reversed list, [5, 4, 2, 1]. Every comparison swaps and all 3 passes run: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 comparisons, the full n(n - 1) / 2. Array is now [1, 2, 4, 5].
Takeaway: about n² / 2 comparisons in the worst case makes bubble sort O(n²); only a list that is already sorted lets it stop after its first pass, O(n).

quiz_full.explanation: A sorted list needs one pass with no swaps: 4 comparisons for 5 items instead of 10.

scenes.narration: How do you remove a node from the middle without breaking the chain? Think of it like unlinking a paperclip from a chain.
Our list has head pointing to 10, which links to 20, 30, and 40, ending with null.
We start at the head and move to 10. 10 points to 20, so we keep going to find our target 30.
We move to 20. 20 points to 30, our target, so 20 is the node right before it and we stop.
20's next pointer now points to 40, so 30 is skipped and no longer reachable. The list is now head -> 10 -> 20 -> 40 -> null.
We stop at the node before the target, not at the target itself, because only the previous node holds the next pointer we need to change.
A singly linked list has no backward pointers, so while walking we always look at the node ahead to see if it is the target.
Changing that single pointer is the whole deletion: no other node moves or changes.
If we try to delete 99 which is not in the list, the pointers stay the same and nothing changes.
Edge case: if the target is the head, there is no node before it, so we simply move the head pointer to the second node.
Edge case: if the target is the tail, the node before it becomes the new tail and its next pointer is set to null.
To delete a middle node, walk to the node before it and update that node's next pointer to skip the target and connect to the following node.

quiz_full.question: In the linked list head -> 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> null, after you delete 30, what does node 20 point to?
quiz_full.explanation: 20 was the node before 30, so its next pointer is rewired past 30 to 40. The list becomes head -> 10 -> 20 -> 40 -> null.

quiz_full.question: When you delete 30 from the linked list head -> 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> null, which node's next pointer changes?
quiz_full.explanation: Only the node before 30, which is 20, changes its next pointer; 30 is skipped and no other node moves.

quiz_full.question: If you instead delete the tail 40 from the linked list head -> 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> null, what does 30 point to afterwards?
quiz_full.explanation: 30 becomes the new tail, so its next pointer is set to null.
